title: Market hours and extended hours

facts.quote: Regular trading hours for stocks traded on exchanges and certain other markets are from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
facts.claim: Regular trading hours for US stocks are 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

facts.quote: The duration of extended-hours trading sessions varies between markets and trading venues.
facts.claim: How long extended-hours sessions run differs from one market or venue to the next.

facts.quote: However, during extended-hours trading there generally is less trading interest and therefore less price competition for most stocks, which may raise trading costs, increase uncertainty with respect to prevailing prices, or make it more difficult to execute trades.
facts.claim: Extended hours usually have less trading interest and price competition, which can raise costs, blur the real price and make fills harder.

facts.quote: The prices of some stocks traded during extended-hours trading may not reflect the prices of those stocks during regular hours, either at the end of the regular trading session or upon the opening of regular trading the next business day.
facts.claim: An extended-hours price may not match the regular-session close or the next day's open.

facts.quote: Extended-hours trading systems are not linked together. As a result, depending on the extended-hours trading system or the time of day, the price of a stock displayed on one trading system may not reflect the price of the same stock
facts.claim: Extended-hours venues are not linked, so two of them can show different prices for the same stock at the same time.

facts.quote: Companies may announce important news or financial information outside of regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Companies may release important news and financial results outside regular trading hours.

facts.quote: These announcements, combined with other extended-hours trading risks, may lead to significant price changes in these companies’ stocks during extended hours trading.
facts.claim: News released out of hours, on thin trading, can move a stock sharply in extended hours.

facts.quote: The reduced level of trading interest in extended-hours trading generally results in wider spreads between the bid and ask prices for a stock or no quotes at all.
facts.claim: Extended-hours spreads are usually wider, and sometimes there is no quote at all.

facts.quote: With respect to extended-hours trading, many brokerage firms currently accept only limit orders
facts.claim: Many brokers accept only limit orders in extended hours.

facts.quote: For stocks with limited trading activity, investors may find greater price fluctuations than they typically would see during regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Thinly traded stocks can swing more in extended hours than they do in the regular session.

facts.quote: Regular trading hours for listed stocks, as defined by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), are from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: FINRA, citing the SEC, puts regular trading hours for listed stocks at 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Trading activity that takes place early in the morning before regular trading begins is commonly referred to as pre-market trading.
facts.claim: Trading in the morning before the regular session opens is called pre-market trading.

facts.quote: Trading that occurs later in the day after regular trading ends is known as post-market or after-hours trading.
facts.claim: Trading after the regular session ends is called after-hours (or post-market) trading.

facts.quote: Pre-market trading is typically defined as taking place from 7 – 9:30 a.m. ET and after-hours trading from 4 – 8 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: FINRA's typical definition: pre-market 7 to 9:30 a.m. ET, after hours 4 to 8 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Trading beyond these time periods, such as during the overnight hours from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, has also more recently been made available to retail investors for certain stocks.
facts.claim: Overnight trading, 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, is now open to retail investors in certain stocks.

facts.quote: Any activity that takes place outside of regular trading hours, whether in the pre-market, after-hours or overnight periods, is generally referred to as extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: Pre-market, after-hours and overnight trading together are called extended-hours trading.

facts.quote: Despite the increasing amount of extended-hours trading activity, that activity is still dwarfed by the tens of millions of transactions that typically take place during regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Extended-hours trading is growing but is still dwarfed by regular-hours trading.

facts.quote: As a result, your order may be executed partially or not at all. If it's executed, it might not be at a competitive price compared to regular trading hours.
facts.claim: In extended hours an order may fill partly or not at all, and a fill may be at a worse price than in regular hours.

facts.quote: Because fewer trades occur during extended hours, stocks might be vulnerable to wider swings.
facts.claim: With fewer trades, stocks can swing more in extended hours.

facts.quote: key corporate events, such as earnings or other significant announcements, which normally take place during the extended-hours period.
facts.claim: Earnings and other big company announcements normally come out during extended hours.

facts.quote: However, trading might become smoother once investors have had time to review and absorb more information about the results and regular trading hours resume.
facts.claim: After an out-of-hours earnings move, trading can settle once people digest the results and the regular session opens.

facts.quote: During regular trading hours, brokerage firms are generally required by SEC rules to fill customer orders for listed stocks at the best price at the time
facts.claim: In regular hours, brokers are generally required to fill orders in listed stocks at the best price available at the time.

facts.quote: However, the NBBO is only published during regular trading hours, so this requirement doesn’t apply to extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: That best-price requirement does not apply in extended hours.

facts.quote: The share prices recorded at 4 p.m. on the exchanges on a given day are considered the official closing prices for that day, regardless of what happens during extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: The 4 p.m. price is the official close, whatever trades in extended hours.

facts.quote: The next day’s opening prices are generated based on supply and demand for the securities at or around the time markets open.
facts.claim: The next day's opening price comes from supply and demand at the open.

facts.quote: Rules among brokerage firms about when and how customers can participate in extended-hours trading may vary.
facts.claim: Each broker sets its own rules for when and how you can trade in extended hours.

facts.quote: For Nasdaq, pre-market trading hours are 4:00 am to 9:30 am, Eastern Time Zone. After hours runs from 4:00 pm to 8:00 pm, Eastern Time Zone.
facts.claim: At Nasdaq, pre-market runs 4:00 to 9:30 a.m. ET and after hours runs 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Certain brokers have different pre-market and after hours trading times.
facts.claim: Some brokers use different extended-hours times than the exchange.

facts.quote: The volatility tends to be much higher, and there is less liquidity, meaning that fewer people are trading and that prices tend to move much more dramatically.
facts.claim: Extended hours have higher volatility and less liquidity: fewer people trading and bigger price moves.

walkthroughs.title: Three sessions, one clock
steps: The regular session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern. That's where the crowd is.
Before it is pre-market, after it is after hours. Some stocks trade overnight too. All of that is extended hours.
On Nasdaq, pre-market starts at 4:00 a.m. and after hours runs to 8:00 p.m.
Your broker sets its own window, often a shorter one. We don't buy outside regular hours anyway.

walkthroughs.title: Thin prints and official prints
steps: Outside regular hours, far fewer people trade. Spreads widen, and one order can swing the price.
Those trades still count in the day's volume. They carry a T flag.
But they don't set the day's official high, low or last price.
The close is the 4 p.m. price, whatever trades after. On Nasdaq, the auctions set the official open and close.

walkthroughs.title: Why gaps show up at the open
steps: Earnings and other big news mostly land while the regular session is closed.
It reprices on thin trading and opens well off yesterday's close. That's the gap. On earnings, it's an earnings gapper.
Here's the catch. Many brokers take only limit orders outside regular hours, so your stop waits for the open.
Then it triggers and becomes a market order. It fills wherever the stock trades, which can be well past your stop.

questions.q: You're setting up your trading day. When does the regular session for US stocks open and close?
questions.why: 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern, wherever you live. That's the regular session, and it's where the real crowd trades. Everything outside it, pre-market, after hours and overnight, is extended hours. If you're not on Eastern time, convert it once and set your alarms off that. Your whole day runs on that clock: the open you watch and the close you measure from.
questions.lesson_line: 9:30 to 4:00 Eastern. That's the session. Everything else is extended hours.

wrong.9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. your time: The clock is Eastern Time for everybody. If you live somewhere else, convert it.
wrong.4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET: That's Nasdaq's whole day, pre-market start to after-hours end. The regular session is just the middle of it.
wrong.9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET: Those are office hours. The bell rings at 9:30 a.m. and the close is 4:00 p.m.

questions.simple: Regular hours run 9:30 to 4:00 Eastern Time, wherever you live, and everything else is extended hours.

reasons: fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Trading in the hours just before the 9:30 a.m. open is called ___ trading.
questions.why: Pre-market. FINRA calls trading early in the morning, before regular trading begins, pre-market trading. Trading after the close is after-hours trading. Overnight trading runs from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, so it does not sit just before the open. Core is the NYSE's name for the regular session itself.
questions.lesson_line: Pre-market comes before the open. After hours comes after the close.
questions.simple: It is called pre-market trading, because it happens in the morning before regular trading begins.

questions.q: Most of a normal day's trading in a stock happens before the open or after the close.
questions.why: False. The crowd shows up from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET. Extended-hours trading keeps growing, but regular hours still dwarf it. That matters because a deep market is what gets you a fair fill. More buyers and sellers means tighter spreads and prices you can trust. Outside those hours you're in a much thinner market, with wider spreads and sometimes no quote at all. That's why we do our buying in the regular session.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd trades 9:30 to 4:00. Outside that, you're in a much thinner market.
questions.simple: False. Most trading happens in regular hours, and that deep crowd is what gets you a fair price.

questions.q: When do companies usually release their earnings reports?
questions.why: Outside regular trading hours. FINRA says earnings and other big company announcements normally come out in the extended-hours period. Schwab and Fidelity say many companies report after the regular close. So the first trades on the news happen in extended hours, not in the regular session. Extended hours also include the pre-market, before the open.
questions.lesson_line: Big news lands while the regular session is shut. That's when the stock starts to reprice.

wrong.During regular trading hours: Not usually. Many companies report after the regular close, so the first reaction trades after hours.
wrong.Right at the 9:30 a.m. open: The news usually comes out outside the session, not at the bell. By the open it's already out.
wrong.Mid-session, with trading halted: Not usually. FINRA says earnings normally come out in the extended-hours period, when the regular session is already shut.

questions.simple: Usually outside regular hours, so the first trades on the news happen after hours or before the next open.

questions.q: Your broker's pre-market hours are set by the exchange, so they start at Nasdaq's 4:00 a.m. ET.
questions.why: False. Nasdaq's own pre-market starts at 4:00 a.m. ET, but brokers set their own windows. Fidelity takes pre-market orders from 7:00 a.m. to 9:28 a.m. ET. Schwab's pre-market runs 7:00 to 9:25 a.m., and its after hours starts at 4:05 p.m. Check your own broker's hours.
questions.lesson_line: The exchange's hours are not your hours. Check what your broker allows.
questions.simple: False, brokers set their own hours, and Fidelity's and Schwab's pre-market sessions start at 7:00 a.m.

reasons: exchange and broker hours change over time (Nasdaq adds a 9 p.m. to 4 a.m. session from 2026-12-06)

questions.q: It's 6:15 p.m. and you want to place an order in after hours. Many brokers take only one order type then. Which one?
questions.why: Limit orders. Many brokers take nothing else out of hours, Fidelity and Schwab included. Schwab won't even run your stop orders then. The reason is the thin market. Few buyers and sellers means wide spreads, so a market order could fill way off the last price. A limit caps what you pay. For us it's simpler still. We don't make new buys out of hours. We buy in the regular session, with market orders, where the crowd is.
questions.lesson_line: Out of hours, many brokers take only limits. We don't buy then anyway.

wrong.Market orders: In a thin market a market order can fill far from the last price. Many brokers won't take one out of hours.
wrong.Stop orders: Schwab doesn't run stops in extended hours, and Fidelity takes limit orders only.
wrong.Stop-limit orders: Close, but a stop-limit isn't a plain limit. Fidelity and Schwab take only limit orders out of hours.

questions.simple: A limit order. Out of hours the market is thin, so many brokers only take orders that cap your price.

reasons: broker order rules vary and can change ('many', not all)

questions.q: You're on a 5-minute chart, regular hours only. How many bars make up one full trading day?
questions.why: 78. The session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., six and a half hours. Times 60, that's 390 minutes. Divide 390 by 5 and you get 78 bars. Here's why you care. If one day shows more than 78, your chart is drawing extended hours too. Those extra bars are thin, so know which view you're on before you compare one day's volume or high with another's.
questions.lesson_line: More than 78 five-minute bars in a day means your chart is showing extended hours.
questions.simple: 78 bars. The session is six and a half hours, and each bar covers 5 minutes.

deeper.trap: Many charts can draw pre-market and after-hours bars too. If one day shows more than 78 five-minute bars, those extra bars are extended hours. They are thin: extended-hours trading is still dwarfed by regular-hours trading. Know which view you are on before you compare a day's volume or its high with another day's.

reasons: computed key

wrong.72 bars: You used six hours. The session is six and a half, 9:30 to 4:00.
wrong.84 bars: You used seven hours, as if the session opened at 9:00.
wrong.390 bars: That's the minutes, not the bars. Divide 390 by 5.

questions.q: You pull up a 5-minute chart and see a big bar stamped 4:35 p.m. ET. Which session is that bar from?
questions.why: After hours. The bell rang at 4:00 p.m. ET, and after hours runs from 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. Overnight doesn't start until 8:00. So that big bar formed in a thin market. When hardly anyone's trading, a few orders can paint a big candle. Don't read it like a regular-hours bar. Check the time stamp first, and know whether your chart has extended hours turned on.
questions.lesson_line: Read the time stamp first. A 4:35 p.m. bar is after hours, thin and easy to push around.

wrong.Regular session: The regular session ended at 4:00 p.m. ET. This bar came after the bell.
wrong.Pre-market: Pre-market is the morning, before the 9:30 a.m. open.
wrong.Overnight: Overnight trading starts at 8 p.m. ET. This bar is hours earlier.

questions.simple: After hours. The regular session ends at 4:00 p.m., and after hours runs to 8:00 p.m.

reasons: session times change over time (new overnight session from 2026-12-06)

questions.q: It's Friday, November 27, 2026, the day after Thanksgiving. You plan to sell into the close. When does the regular session end?
questions.why: 1:00 p.m. ET. The day after Thanksgiving is a half day, so the bell rings three hours early. Thanksgiving itself, November 26, is closed. If you're waiting for 4:00 to sell into the close, you'll miss it. Eligible options close at 1:15 p.m. that day, but stocks are done at 1:00. Pull up the exchange holiday calendar each year and mark the half days before they sneak up on you.
questions.lesson_line: Know your half days. The day after Thanksgiving, the bell rings at 1:00 p.m.

wrong.4:00 p.m. ET: That's a normal day. This Friday is a half day, and stocks close at 1:00 p.m.
wrong.It's closed all day: That's Thanksgiving itself, Thursday, November 26. Friday trades, then closes early.
wrong.1:15 p.m. ET: That's when eligible options close. Stocks close at 1:00 p.m.

questions.simple: The session ends early at 1:00 p.m. ET, because the day after Thanksgiving is a half day.

questions.story: A stock closes at $60 on Tuesday. At 4:05 p.m. it reports earnings far above forecasts. On Wednesday it opens at $66.
questions.q: Wednesday this stock opens at $66, an earnings gapper. Where did that gap come from?
choices: News that came out after the close
The after-hours price became the close
The exchange reset the price overnight
Pre-market trades became the open price
questions.answer: News that came out after the close
questions.why: The earnings news, out after the close. A stock that gaps on its report is what we call an earnings gapper. Tuesday's close stays $60, the 4 p.m. price. The report hit at 4:05, buyers piled in overnight, and Wednesday's open came from that demand. $66 against $60 is six dollars, ten percent on the close. A gap like that, on real news, is worth putting on your radar. It isn't a buy by itself.
questions.lesson_line: A gap on earnings is an earnings gapper. The news hit while the regular session was shut.

wrong.The after-hours price became the close: The close stays Tuesday's 4 p.m. price. After-hours trades don't change it.
wrong.The exchange reset the price overnight: Nobody resets it by hand. The open comes from buyers and sellers at the open.
wrong.Pre-market trades became the open price: Pre-market trades don't set the open. The opening auction at 9:30 does, from supply and demand.

questions.simple: The earnings report came out after the close, buyers built up overnight, and the stock opened well above $60.

reasons: fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: Your stock trades at $80.00 at 4:00 p.m. At 6:30 p.m. it prints $83.00. What's the official close for the day?
questions.why: $80.00, the 4:00 p.m. price. The closing auction at 4:00 sets the official close, and nothing after hours changes it. The $83.00 print is a real trade, just a thin after-hours one. This matters for your math. Tomorrow's gap and the day's percent change both start from that $80.00 close. Measure from $83.00 and every number you work out is off.
questions.lesson_line: After-hours prints are real trades. The close is still the 4:00 p.m. price.

wrong.$83.00: That's an after-hours print. Extended hours don't change the official close.
After hours can run to 8:00 p.m., but the close was already set at 4:00.
wrong.$81.50: The close isn't a blend of prices. It's the 4:00 p.m. price.

questions.simple: $80.00, because the 4:00 p.m. price is the official close, whatever trades after hours.

reasons: fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: Your stock closed yesterday at $40.00. This morning it opens at $44.00. How big is the gap, in percent?
questions.why: 10%, a gap up. You always measure from yesterday's close. $44.00 minus $40.00 is $4.00. Divide $4.00 by the $40.00 close and you get 10%. Use percent, not dollars. Four dollars on a $40 stock is a big move. On a stock trading in the hundreds it's a blip. Percent lets you compare any two gaps, and that's how we read every chart.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a gap from yesterday's close to today's open, in percent.
questions.simple: The gap is 10%, because the $44.00 open is $4.00 above the $40.00 close.

reasons: computed key

wrong.9.1%: You divided by the $44.00 open. Divide by yesterday's $40.00 close.
wrong.4%: That's the $4.00 dollar gap read as a percent.
wrong.110%: You divided the open by the close and forgot to subtract one.

questions.story: At 3:58 p.m. you place a day limit order to sell at $25.00. It doesn't fill by the 4:00 p.m. close. At 4:30 p.m. the stock trades at $25.20.
questions.q: What most likely happened to your sell order?
choices: It turned into a market order
questions.why: It cancelled at the close. At most brokers, a day order that hasn't filled by 4:00 p.m. is done. It doesn't carry into after hours or the next day. So the $25.20 print at 4:30 doesn't help you, even though it's above your $25.00 limit. If you still want out after the bell, send a new limit order marked for extended hours. Some brokers, like Schwab, make you pick the session on every order. Check how yours handles it.
questions.lesson_line: A plain day order stops at the close. To trade after the bell, mark the order for extended hours.

wrong.It sold at $25.20 after hours: A plain day order doesn't carry into after hours. You'd have to mark the order for that session.
wrong.It waits for tomorrow's open: A day order is good for one day only. It doesn't roll to tomorrow.
wrong.It turned into a market order: That's what a stop does when it's hit. An unfilled day limit just cancels.

questions.simple: It cancelled at the close. A plain day order ends with regular hours and doesn't carry into after hours.

deeper.trap: The $25.20 print at 4:30 p.m. is above your $25.00 limit, so it feels like you should have sold. You didn't. A plain day order had already cancelled at the close. If you want an after-hours fill, enter a new order and mark it for the extended session.

reasons: broker order rules vary ('generally'; some sell day orders that include extended hours)

questions.q: Out of hours, your broker still has to fill you at the best price shown across all venues.
questions.why: False. Nobody owes you the best price out of hours. From 9:30 to 4:00, the SEC's best-price rule covers you. Outside those hours it doesn't. Extended-hours venues aren't linked, and nothing stops your order trading through a better price somewhere else. So you fill where your order lands, even if another venue shows better. If you trade out of hours, use a limit and set it from prices you can see. It's one more reason we don't buy out there.
questions.lesson_line: Out of hours you get the price where your order lands, not the best price anywhere.
questions.simple: False. The best-price rule only covers regular hours, so out of hours your order fills wherever it lands.

deeper.trap: After hours, the price on your screen may come from one venue while a better price sits on another. With no link between venues and no trade-through protection, your limit order fills where it lands, not at the best price anywhere. Set your limit from the prices you can actually see, and don't assume a better fill elsewhere.

reasons: rule tied to SIP hours that change from 2026-12-06
fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.story: At 7:40 a.m. ET a stock prints $26.00. It closed yesterday at $24.00. Only a few hundred shares have traded so far.
questions.q: What's that $26.00 print telling you?
choices: A thin print, not a firm price
The price it will open at
A cue to buy at market now
A solid price, a real trade
questions.answer: A thin print, not a firm price
questions.why: A thin print, not a firm price. Only a few hundred shares have traded, and in a market that thin one order can move the price. It's two bucks over yesterday's close, which looks exciting. But an extended-hours price may not hold into the open. Put it on your radar and let the regular session show you if the buyers are real. We don't buy before the open anyway.
questions.lesson_line: I treat a 7:40 a.m. print as a hint, not a verdict. The open is the real test.

wrong.The price it will open at: Nothing promises that. An extended-hours price may not match the open.
wrong.A cue to buy at market now: Many brokers won't take a market order this early, and we make no new buys before the open.
wrong.A solid price, a real trade: It's a real trade, but on a few hundred shares. One order can push a market that thin around.

questions.simple: A thin early print, since one order can move it with so few shares trading. Wait for the open.

deeper.trap: An early print can look like a head start. Buying it is the trap: our rule is no new buys outside regular hours. Out of hours, an order may fill only partly, or at a worse price than in regular hours. The open comes from supply and demand at the open, so let it speak first.

reasons: fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: A stock trades heavy in the pre-market on news. Those shares count toward its consolidated volume for the day.
questions.why: True. Pre-market and after-hours trades are real trades. They count in the day's consolidated volume, the total across every venue. So on a news day, part of that big volume number traded before the bell, in a thin market. Before you call it heavy buying, check how much came in the regular session, when the full crowd was in.
questions.lesson_line: Big pre-market volume is real volume. It counts in the day's total.
questions.simple: True. Pre-market trades are real trades, and they count in the day's total volume.

reasons: data-plan rules tied to the December 2026 extended-hours change
fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: A trade at 7:40 a.m. can set a stock's consolidated high for the day.
questions.why: False. Trades outside 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. carry the T sale condition and are not last-sale eligible. The UTP plan marks trades from 12:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. as Form T, so a 7:40 a.m. trade is one. In both consolidated data plans' tables, a T trade does not update the consolidated high, low or last price. It is still a real trade. It just does not count toward the consolidated high.
questions.lesson_line: A pre-market high is a real trade, but it doesn't set the day's consolidated high.
questions.simple: False, a trade at 7:40 a.m. is outside regular hours, so it does not set the day's consolidated high.

deeper.trap: A stock spikes in the pre-market, then never trades that high in the regular session. The spike is a real trade. It does not set the consolidated high, so the day's consolidated high can sit below it. Before you mark a level from that high, check whether your tools include extended-hours trades.

reasons: data-plan rules tied to the December 2026 extended-hours change
fixed before (checker, 2026-11-09)

questions.story: You own a stock that closed at $50, with a sell stop at $48. Your broker runs stops in regular hours only. Bad company news after the close sends it to $42. It opens next morning at $43.
questions.q: Where does your stop most likely fill?
questions.why: Near $43, at the open. Your broker only runs stops in regular hours, so nothing happens after the close. At the open the stock trades at $43, already under your $48 stop. The stop triggers, turns into a market order and sells at the going price. That's about five dollars a share worse than you planned. A stop price is a trigger, not a promise. That's why a tight stop never earns you a monster position. It can't catch an overnight gap.
questions.lesson_line: A stop can't catch an overnight gap. News can open the stock right through it.

wrong.At $48, your stop price: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill. The stock opened below it.
wrong.Near $42, in after hours: Your broker doesn't run stops after hours. Nothing fired until the regular session.
wrong.Nowhere, the gap skipped it: A gap doesn't skip a stop. At the open it triggers and sells near $43.

questions.simple: Near $43 at the open. The stock opened under your stop, so the stop sold at the going price.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating $48 as your worst case. A stop price is a trigger, not a floor. News opened the stock below the stop. So the stop fired at the open and filled near the going price, here near $43. A triggered stop can fill far from its stop price.

reasons: broker stop rules vary (the story states the broker's rule)
touches the owner's gap rule B20 and real-stop rule D41 (owner flag)

questions.story: A stock you follow reports earnings at 4:05 p.m. and falls 9% after hours. The quote is wide, and only small trades are printing.
questions.q: What's this telling you right now?
choices: Real news, but a thin, shaky price
Real news, so the drop holds
questions.answer: Real news, but a thin, shaky price
questions.why: Real news, but a thin, shaky price. The quote is wide and only small trades are printing. That's a thin market, and a thin market's price can be way off. The news is real, so don't wave it off. But that 9% isn't settled, and the open may land higher or lower. Once people digest the results and the regular session opens, the full crowd weighs in. That's the price I'd trust. Until then it stays on your radar, and you do nothing.
questions.lesson_line: Respect the news, not the exact after-hours price. The open is where the full market weighs in.

wrong.The close is now 9% lower: The close is still the 4 p.m. price. After-hours trading doesn't change it.
wrong.Real news, so the drop holds: The news is real, but nothing says the price holds. After-hours prices may not match the next open.
wrong.Just noise the open erases: Real news can move a stock hard out of hours, and nothing says the open undoes it.

questions.simple: The news is real, but the after-hours price is thin and shaky. The open may land somewhere else.

deeper.counter: Sometimes the after-hours drop is only the start, and the open lands even lower once the full market weighs in. The point is not that the price will bounce. A thin after-hours price is a rough guess, in either direction, until regular hours resume.

reasons: story no longer has the member holding through earnings (rulebook B22)

questions.story: A stock you're watching hits your buy point at 7:45 a.m. ET, in the pre-market. Your broker takes pre-market orders.
questions.q: It's 7:45 and the stock is through your buy point. What's the play?
choices: Buy now with a limit order
Buy now with a market order
Skip the stock for the day
questions.why: Wait for the regular session. We make no new buys outside 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET, even when your broker takes the order. At 7:45 the market's thin. Spreads are wide, fills can be poor, and the price may not hold into the open. Keep it on your radar with an alert set. If it's still through your buy point once the session opens, that's where we get involved, with a market order. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, LOD.
questions.simple: Wait for the regular session. We make no new buys outside regular hours, when the market is thin.
questions.lesson_line: A pre-market price can tempt you. We wait for the open to buy.

wrong.Buy now with a limit order: Your broker may take it, but we make no new buys before 9:30. The pre-market is too thin.
wrong.Buy now with a market order: That's how we enter, but only in the regular session. Out here a market order can fill far off the price you see.
wrong.Skip the stock for the day: Too far. We only rule out buying before the open. The trade can still come once the session starts.

reasons: house rule E58 (and E57 in a wrong note)

No question keys one start time for pre-market in general. Every time in a question names the venue or the broker, and q05 teaches that windows differ.

Longer hours are coming: Nasdaq (f33, 23/5 hub) and NYSE Arca (NYSE extended-hours FAQ, August 2026) plan a 9:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. ET overnight session from December 6, 2026, four weeks after as_of, pending SEC approvals and SIP readiness; the CTA FAQ (v1.2) gives the same date. The regular session, its opening and closing auctions (f32) and the 'T' / not-last-sale rule (f50) are unchanged by the plan. Re-read the Nasdaq hub and FINRA's page after December 6, 2026.

A chart vendor can still draw extended-hours bars its own way, so no question claims what a member's chart shows beyond q07's arithmetic (regular hours only, 78 five-minute bars).

No question asks whether a gap filled or whether the range cleared the prior day.

q14 after December 6, 2026 (checker): the SIPs move to about 23 hours, so FINRA's 'the NBBO is only published during regular trading hours' may change. Reg NMS Rule 600(b)(105) (f74, eCFR up to date as of 11/05/2026) defines a trade-through as one 'during regular trading hours', so trade-through protection still stops at 4:00 p.m. unless the rule changes. Best execution (a broker's duty of care) still applies out of hours; q14 is about a best price across venues, which no rule promises then. Re-read FINRA's page and Rule 600 after December 6, 2026.
